definition: The tradition that traces its teaching to Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, and to the communities that formed around him. It is practised in many forms across Asia and beyond, with Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana as broad families.
A title meaning awakened one, given to Siddhartha Gautama after his awakening under the bodhi tree. It is not a personal name, and the tradition recognises other buddhas before and after him.
The tree at Bodh Gaya under which Siddhartha sat on the night of his awakening. A descendant grown from a cutting taken to Sri Lanka stands at the site today and is visited by pilgrims.

The tempter and lord of death in Buddhist narrative, who tries to prevent the Buddha's awakening and later returns to trouble the community. He is read both as a cosmic being and as the personification of craving, fear and doubt.

A genre of stories about the Buddha's previous births, collected in the Pali canon and in other traditions. In them the Bodhisatta appears as a king, an animal or a merchant, and each story closes with an identification of the characters.
The teaching of the Buddha, and also the truth it points to and the way of life that follows from it. The word carries different shades of meaning in different Buddhist schools and languages.
The community of Buddhist practitioners, especially the ordained monks and nuns. Taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha is the basic declaration of a Buddhist life.

The Buddha's cousin and longtime attendant, remembered for his memory and for reciting the discourses at the first council. His name is associated with the opening formula of the suttas, 'Thus have I heard'.
The grieving mother in a story preserved in the Dhammapada commentary, who is sent to find mustard seed from a house untouched by death. Her search becomes a lesson in shared loss.
A murderer who became a Buddhist monk after the Buddha confronted him, remembered in the Angulimala Sutta. His story is one of the tradition's hardest tests of forgiveness and change.
